div.p: The Iriomote cat (Prionailurus bengalensis iriomotensis) is a critically endangered wild felid endemic to Iriomotejima Island in the Ryukyu Archipelago, Japan (Fig. 1). Its population is approximately 100, and it is the only native cat on this island (Izawa et al. 2009). The Iriomote cat shows very low genetic variation (Johnson et al. 1999), and it is mainly threatened by habitat destruction and vehicles (Izawa et al. 2009). Further, domestic cats (Felis catus) in some areas, may compete with Iriomote cats for habitat resources (Watanabe 2003).

Because intrusive methods can adversely affect endangered carnivore populations (Morell 1995), studies on their basic ecology should be conducted with minimal human disturbance. This analysis was used to identify nucleotide substitutions in order to deterble confounding results (Fig. 2). The black rat (Rattus rattus) is the prey of both felids, while the wild boar (Sus scrofa) is eaten only by the Iriomote cat (Watanabe et al. 2003). Because sequences of target DNA regions were unavailable in the databases for the fruit bat (Pteropus dasymallus yaeyamae), a species consumed exclusively by the Iriomote cat (Watanabe et al. 2003), its DNA (n = 2) was used to test for any confounding results.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: the scat samples were of Iriomote cats. Mills et al. (2000) derived from both the Iriomote cat and the domestic cat. This ambiguous result could be attributed to experimental contamination or the latrine site being used by both cats.

According to Watanabe et al. (2003), distribution of the scats of the domestic cat mainly depends on waste disposal sites. Therefore, one reason for the virtual absence of scat samples of the domestic cat may be attributable to the absence of waste disposal sites near the survey areas.

Sequence alignment of the target region within the 16S rRNA gene and the Zfx and Zfy genes of mammals found on Iriomote-jima Island with those of the Iriomote cat and the domestic cat revealed high genetic variation among these species. By testing more scat samples, PCR-RFLP of the sexlinked genes Zfx and Zfy could be used to identify sexand conservation.
